title: Bottom Standing Still? Rolling Explained Simply | Class 11 Physics
description:
Look at a photo of a moving bicycle: the spokes at the top are a blur, but the spokes at the bottom are sharp. A rolling tyre leaves a clean print, not a smear. Is the bottom of a moving wheel really standing still? In this animated lesson for Class 11 Physics (Chapter 6, System of Particles and Rotational Motion) we learn rolling motion. Note: rolling is not in the current rationalised NCERT book; it is in the JEE Advanced syllabus (rolling without slipping).

On a live motion notebook a wheel rolls without slipping while a gold mark on its rim traces a cycloid, the readout tracks v, omega and the mark's speed, and a graph shows that speed rising to 2v at the top and falling to zero at the bottom. A slow-mo replay freezes the wheel and adds the forward velocity of the centre to the spin velocity at the top, the front and the bottom. We see link by link why v = R omega, build the speed of any point step by step (the wheel turns about the contact point), compare rolling with skidding, and work out the speeds on a cycle wheel. Then the exam trap (the contact point is at rest but still accelerates), an original JEE Main pattern question, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

Made for NCERT, CBSE, ISC (CISCE) and PUC (Karnataka) Class 11 students, and for JEE Main, JEE Advanced and NEET preparation.

In this video:
0:00 Why is the bottom of a moving wheel sharp in a photo?
0:25 Rolling = translation + rotation, v = R omega
0:49 Motion notebook: a rolling wheel, its cycloid and the speed of a rim mark
1:16 Pause and think: centre or top, which is faster?
1:32 Slow-mo replay: top 2v, bottom 0, front root 2 v
1:57 Why v = R omega, link by link
2:17 Speed of any point in five steps
2:59 Rolling vs skidding + pause and think
3:31 Worked example: a cycle wheel at 5 m/s
4:07 Exam trap: the contact point still accelerates
4:29 Practice question (JEE Main pattern)
5:07 Recap and three questions to answer

Next episode: Kinetic Energy of Rolling Motion. A ring, a disc and a ball race down the same slope from the same height. Who wins, and why?
